prompt: What makes two `.go` files part of the same package?

choices.text: One of them imports the other
choices.why: A file never imports a file; `top.go` used `Counts` with no import at all.

choices.text: They sit in the same directory
choices.why: Right. The directory is the package, and its files must all give the same package clause.

choices.text: Their file names start with the package name
choices.why: File names mean nothing to the compiler: `count.go` and `top.go` both belong to `text`.

choices.text: They are listed together in `go.mod`
choices.why: `go.mod` names the module and its requirements, not its packages or files.

prompt: The module `example.com/shop` has a package in the directory `store/price`. What does another package write to import it?

choices.text: `"store/price"`
choices.why: A path with no dot in its first element is looked for in the standard library, as lesson 38 showed.

choices.text: `"example.com/shop/price"`
choices.why: The whole directory goes after the module path, `store` included.

choices.text: `"example.com/shop/store/price"`
choices.why: Right: the module path from `go.mod`, followed by the directory.

choices.text: `"price"`, the package's name
choices.why: The name is what code writes before a dot; the import line writes the path.

prompt: The files of `math/rand/v2` begin with `package ___`, so a file that imports it calls `rand.N`.
`count.go` imports `strings`. A new file `text/f.go`, in the same package, calls `strings.Fields` and imports nothing. What happens?
hint: Do imports belong to the package or to the file?

choices.text: It compiles: the package already imports `strings`
choices.why: Names declared in a package are shared between its files; imports are not.

choices.text: It is refused with `undefined: strings`
choices.why: Right. Each file imports what it uses, as `top.go` imported `cmp` and `slices` for itself.

choices.text: It compiles, and `go vet` asks for the import
choices.why: This one never gets as far as `vet`: the compiler cannot resolve `strings` in that file.

choices.text: It is refused with `found packages text and f`
choices.why: That error needs two package clauses; `f.go` says `package text` like the others.

prompt: Which of these can sit together in one directory? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `a.go` and `b.go`, both saying `package text`
choices.why: Yes, like `count.go` and `top.go`.

choices.text: `text.go` saying `package text` and `words.go` saying `package words`
choices.why: Refused: `found packages text (count.go) and words (words.go)`.

choices.text: Files called anything at all, all saying `package main`
choices.why: Yes. File names mean nothing to the compiler; the package clause is what must agree.

choices.text: Two programs, each a file with `package main` and its own `func main`
choices.why: Both files would be one package with `main` declared twice. Two programs need two directories, as `cmd/` gives them.

prompt: A repository needs two programs, `server` and `migrate`, that share code for reading a database. Which layout follows section 02?
hint: Each program is a `package main` of its own.

choices.text: `server.go` and `migrate.go` in the root, each with `func main`
choices.why: One directory is one package, so the two `main` functions would collide.

choices.text: One `main.go` that checks `os.Args` to decide which program it is
choices.why: That builds one binary, not two; `go install ./cmd/...` gave two because there were two directories.

choices.text: `cmd/server`, `cmd/migrate`, and the shared code in a package beside `cmd`
choices.why: Right, the shape of `wordy`: one directory per program, and the shared package imported by both.

choices.text: Two modules, one per program, each with a copy of the code
choices.why: Copies drift apart; one module with a shared package is what `wordy` did.

prompt: Which of these names, declared in `text`, can `cmd/wordtop` use?

choices.text: `byCount`
choices.why: Lower case, so visible only inside `text`: `cmd/peek` got `undefined: text.byCount`.

choices.text: `Top`
choices.why: Right. It starts with an upper-case letter, so it is exported.

choices.text: `_Top`
choices.why: `_` is not an upper-case letter, so the name is not exported, whatever follows.

choices.text: `entries`
choices.why: An unexported method: `cannot refer to unexported method entries`.

prompt: A name that starts with an upper-case letter is ___, and every package that imports its package can use it.
`cmd/peek` is in the same module as `text`. Why was `c.entries()` still refused?

choices.text: Methods are private to their type unless declared `public`
choices.why: Go has no such keyword; the first letter is the whole rule.

choices.text: `text` is a library and `cmd/peek` is a program
choices.why: A program can use every exported name of a library; `Top` worked from `cmd/wordtop`.

choices.text: A lower-case name is hidden from every other package, and `cmd/peek` is one
choices.why: Right. The boundary is the package, not the module.

choices.text: `entries` is declared in `top.go` and `cmd/peek` imports nothing from that file
choices.why: Nothing imports a file; inside `text`, `count.go` could call `entries` freely.

prompt: A struct `Config` has one field, `host string`, tagged `json:"host"`. `json.Unmarshal` fills a `Config` from `{"host":"db"}`. What do `err` and `cfg.host` hold afterwards?
hint: `count` in section 03 went the same way.

choices.text: `err` is nil and `cfg.host` is `"db"`, because the tag names the key
choices.why: A tag cannot make a field visible to `encoding/json`; `count` stayed 0 with its tag.

choices.text: `err` is nil and `cfg.host` is still `""`
choices.why: Right. The field is skipped in silence; only `go vet` reports the tag on an unexported field.

choices.text: `err` reports that `host` is unexported
choices.why: Both directions returned a nil error in section 03; nothing at run time complains.

choices.text: The program does not compile until `host` is capitalised
choices.why: It compiles and runs; the tag is just a string to the compiler.

prompt: You write a helper that splits one line of a file, used by two functions in the same package and by nothing else. What should it be called?

choices.text: `splitLine`
choices.why: Right. Nothing outside needs it, so it stays out of the API and can be changed freely.

choices.text: `SplitLine`, so that it can be tested and documented later
choices.why: Capitalising makes it a promise to every importer; do it on the day another package needs it.

choices.text: `SplitLine`, since both callers are in different files
choices.why: Files of one package share every name, whatever its case: `top.go` used `Counts` from `count.go`.

choices.text: Either: the case of a name is a matter of style in Go
choices.why: The case is the access rule; `cmd/peek` was refused three times over it.

prompt: Why does Go refuse `fold` importing `text` while `text` imports `fold`?
hint: What has to happen to an imported package before the importer?

choices.text: Two packages of one module may import each other only through `internal`
choices.why: `fold` already is under `internal`, and the cycle was refused anyway.

choices.text: Each must be compiled and initialised before the other, and neither can be first
choices.why: Right: `import cycle not allowed`, whatever the number of packages in the loop.

choices.text: It would make the binary too large
choices.why: Each package is compiled once whatever imports it; size is not the reason.

choices.text: `go vet` reports it as a likely mistake
choices.why: It never reaches `vet`: `go build` refused it with exit status 1.

prompt: Which packages may import `example.com/wordy/internal/fold`?

choices.text: Any package of the module `example.com/wordy`
choices.why: Right: the parent of `internal` is the module's root, so the whole module is inside the tree.

choices.text: Only packages in the directory `internal` itself
choices.why: `text` imports it from outside that directory, and is allowed.

choices.text: Any package in a workspace that lists `wordy`
choices.why: `example.com/other` was in the workspace and was refused.

choices.text: Any package, as long as the names it uses are exported
choices.why: `fold.Word` is exported, and `example.com/other` was still refused.

prompt: In `example.com/wordy`, a package sits at `text/internal/cache`. Which package may import it?
hint: The tree is rooted at the parent of `internal`, which is no longer the module's root.

choices.text: `cmd/wordtop`
choices.why: The rule is about the tree, not the module: `cmd/wordtop` is outside `text`, and is refused.

choices.text: `text` and the packages below it
choices.why: Right. The parent of `internal` is `text`, so only `text` and the packages below it may.

choices.text: Every package of the module, as with `internal/fold`
choices.why: `internal/fold` had the module's root as its parent; this one has `text`.

choices.text: None: `internal` may only sit at the root of a module
choices.why: An `internal` element may appear anywhere in a path; the rule finds its parent wherever it is.

prompt: Put in order what ran in `~/pkgs-init` before and during `main`.
hint: An imported package finishes before its importer starts.

prompt: Match each import line to what it does.

pairs.right: Runs the package's `init` and binds no name
Puts every exported name into the file

right_distractors: Loads the package only when a function first uses it

prompt: `image/png` registers its decoder in a function called ___, which runs by itself when the package is imported.
Which of these does `go build` refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are rules about the graph or the directory; one is about an unused name.

choices.text: Package `a` imports `b`, `b` imports `c`, and `c` imports `a`
choices.why: Yes: a cycle through three packages is a cycle.

choices.text: Importing `crypto/rand` and `math/rand/v2` with no alias
choices.why: Yes: `rand redeclared in this block`.

choices.text: A package whose name differs from the last element of its path
choices.why: Allowed: `math/rand/v2` says `package rand`.

choices.text: A blank import of a package the file never names
choices.why: That is what `_` is for: `image/png` was imported that way and the program ran.

prompt: Ana adds `cmd/wordjson/main.go`, a third program, to `example.com/wordy`. How many lines does `go list ./...` print now?
hint: One line per package, one package per directory with Go files.

prompt: `text` imports `fold`, and a new function in `fold` needs to read a `text.Counts`. Which change compiles and keeps the graph pointing one way?
hint: Something has to move, not the import line.

choices.text: Importing `text` into `fold` with an alias
choices.why: An alias renames the import; the arrow back up is still there, and the cycle is still refused.

choices.text: A blank import of `text` in `fold`, so nothing is named
choices.why: A blank import is still an import, and `fold` could not use `Counts` through it anyway.

choices.text: Letting the function take a `map[string]int`, or moving it into `text`
choices.why: Right. Either removes the arrow from `fold` back to `text`.

choices.text: Moving `fold` out of `internal`
choices.why: `internal` decides who may import `fold`, not whether a cycle is allowed.
